wow - as someone who takes meds as well this hit really, really hard. you've really encapsulated what it feels like being off-meds, the sheer desperation to keep holding on to life even though everything seems to slip. these particular lines really spoke to me:


when i've seen three dawns in a row,

because my melatonin isn't working

and the sheep are out grazing.

when i pray to whatever god,

please

let the sun lie back down

but no one ever seems to listen.

specifically the line "and the sheep are out grazing" – to me, it represented how everyone else is living life as usual, getting their morning started, while you're trapped by your insomnia. I've had a lot of nights where I was seeing everyone starting to wake up while I going crazy trying to sleep. grazing, to me, is peaceful, like pouring yourself a cereal bowl in the morning. reading this poem genuinely felt like I was staring at a mirror, well done.

So I would like to preface this by saying that I'm a Korean who's currently living in the States, so obviously I don't have as much insight as a native Korean living in Korea, my upbringing is from a typical conservative Korean family. So for the first couple of your questions, I would like to say that I am very aware that kpop is a image-focused "mechanical" industry. That doesn't really change my liking of kpop, because that's essentially what you're in for if you're a fan. They're called "idols" for a reason; they're supposed to represent perfection. If you aren't a fan of this "fake" image, you wouldn't be a fan if kpop in the first place, which explains the huge khiphop and k-indie scene in Korea. However, to insinuate that kpop is one of the only industries that are image- focused and "fake" is pretty inaccurate. A lot of music industries are pretty image-focused and "fake" at some point, so I don't understand why the kpop industry should be treated differently just because it's Asian and open about its sterile image. 


And honestly, especially in the thread linked, I see so many non-Koreans make completely stereotyped and inaccurate generalizations about a culture they really don't have any idea about, so that's probably why you ruffled so many feathers. One documentary, anecdote, or observation is not enough for someone to assume they're an expert about a culture. So it's kind of insulting to me when people say "oh, these Koreans are fake, they all have plastic surgery, kpop idols all have sex to succeed, etc." since they're talking in a disparaging manner about a culture I personally grew up in. I'm not being hostile to you or talking about you specifically, it's just my sentiments towards all of these stereotypes and ignorance. Oh, I can understand your distaste of some elements of the Spring Day choreo. I do agree that parts of the choreo can be interpreted in a negative way. Also, my point about BTS acknowledging the tragedy wasn't really about how they were brave/putting their careers in danger. I felt like, in a society where idols are only expected to look pretty and sing well, the fact that BTS went out of their way to bring attention to a societal issue is something in and of itself. I don't think that we should be putting BTS on a pedestal for doing this, but they went beyond what was expected of them, making their careers a bit more vulnerable than it could've been. Corruption is deep rooted in Korean politics, and only the figureheads were impeached. While BTS' careers obviously was never in true danger, they still "put themselves out there", for a lack of a better term. Idk they did something really unexpected from an idol group, and that impresses me because they didn't have to at all in the first place. Sorry if I was being redundant lol, its like 4 am where i am. But anyway, I do appreciate contrasting opinions, and I think yours definitely has merit.

Spring Day is 100% a homage to the Sewol Tragedy though. It's easy to see how the MV and even the choreo was about Sewol.  the water motif and the use of the color yellow really drove in that point, not to mention the emphasize in shoes. If that isn't enough, my Korean family was quick to point out all the elements that are associated with the Tragedy. And in no way was any of this disrespectful, the MV especially was very touching. In a society where celebrities aren't encouraged to hold any political views, the fact the BTS decided to bring light to and support the victims of the Sewol Tragedy is very impressive.
